There is a particular hour in the morning when the world seems to belong only to birds and bakers. I have always loved walking then, before the sun clears the rooftops, when the air has that cool, metallic taste. It is not quiet—the city is never truly quiet—but the sounds are different: a bicycle wheel ticking, the scrape of a shutter opening, the far-off hum of a street-cleaning truck. In that light, ordinary objects become briefly unfamiliar. A row of parked cars looks like a herd of sleeping animals.

We spend so much of our lives inside our own heads, rehearsing conversations or worrying about deadlines, that we forget to look at what is actually in front of us. Noticing small things—the way a cashier arranges coins, the exact shade of green on a new leaf, the weight of a door handle—is not a distraction from life. It is a return to it. Attention is a kind of affection. When you really look at something, even for a second, you are saying that it matters.

Yesterday I saw a bee stumble out of a rose and fly away drunkenly, its legs heavy with pollen. For a moment I envied it: no plans, no self-consciousness, just the simple work of gathering sweetness. Then I remembered I was doing the same thing, in my own way. Walking slowly, gathering small moments, letting them stick to me. That is enough. The world is always offering itself to us.
